proposals.name: Human-expert or human-judgment grounding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reports comparing the method's outputs/performance directly against human performance, or uses human judgments/ratings as validation data or evaluation ground truth. Score 5 if humans are mentioned only as a motivating analogy with no actual comparison or judgment data collected. Score 0 if evaluation is purely automatic-metric-vs-automatic-metric with no human reference point anywhere.
proposals.rationale: R14 reports word-error-rate against professional lipreaders (86.4%/92.9% WER) as the benchmark for its 40.9% result, and R27 collects 206,339 human similarity judgments and R37 uses 11 scientists to score outputs on three criteria -- all dense_high_card_low. This kind of grounding against genuine human performance/judgment is invisible to a scorecard built from generic quality rubrics.

proposals.name: Real-world deployment or competitive validation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method is validated via a real operational deployment, a competitive leaderboard/challenge win, or application to genuine external (non-benchmark-curated) data (e.g. real sensor/rover/production data). Score 5 if the paper merely gestures at 'real-world applicability' without concrete deployment evidence. Score 0 if all validation is confined to standard academic benchmark splits.
proposals.rationale: R15 reports being 'one of the winning entries to the Open Graph Benchmark-Large Scale Challenge at KDD Cup 2021' and R47 tests on data 'gathered by the Curiosity rover that is currently operating on Mars' -- both dense_high_card_low. Neither is a formal 'quality dimension' a scorecard bank is likely to encode, since it is about provenance of validation, not the method's numbers.

proposals.name: Honest reporting of negative or mixed results
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract plainly states that its own method or the field's methods fail, partially fail, or remain unsolved on some dimension, without spinning it as a hidden success. Score 5 if limitations are acknowledged only vaguely ('some challenges remain'). Score 0 if the abstract reports uniformly positive, unqualified success on every claim made.
proposals.rationale: R13 states outright that 'None of the methods is successful with ContextRef... ContextRef remains a challenging benchmark' and R45 poses its central question as genuinely open ('would it be more effective to...') rather than pre-answering it -- both dense_high_card_low. A scorecard built to reward stated accomplishments plausibly penalizes this candor as a weaker 'contribution'.

proposals.name: Meta-scientific rigor about measurement validity itself
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper's core contribution concerns the reliability/validity of measurement or evaluation itself (e.g. reproducibility across seeds/checkpoints, statistical inference frameworks for comparing models, quantified benchmark-compression with reconstruction error) rather than a new task-performance number. Score 5 if this is a minor side-analysis. Score 0 if the paper only reports a new method's task performance with no reflection on measurement reliability.
proposals.rationale: R40 introduces 25 BERT checkpoints plus a 'Multi-Bootstrap' statistical method specifically because 'repeating the pre-training process can lead to substantially different performance,' and R17 distills six benchmarks into metabench and reports RMSE/Spearman-r for how well it reconstructs the originals -- both dense_high_card_low. This class of contribution (rigor about evaluation) is orthogonal to what a fixed quality-criterion bank typically checks for.

proposals.name: Breadth of systematic multi-dataset or multi-domain validation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method/finding is validated across genuinely distinct datasets, domains, or modalities (not just multiple splits of one dataset or one task family), ideally with a stated count. Score 5 if validated on 2-3 closely related datasets within one task type. Score 0 if validated on a single dataset/benchmark.
proposals.rationale: R51 validates against four distinct QA datasets plus a separate entity-typing dataset, and R27 evaluates 611 pretrained models across three different modalities (images, audio, video) with 206K collected judgments -- both dense_high_card_low. Genuine cross-domain breadth is a stronger quality signal than within-domain replication, but a scorecard tallying 'experiments reported' may not distinguish real breadth from repeated narrow validation.

proposals.name: Precise diagnosis of a specific prior-work failure mode
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a specific, mechanistically precise weakness in prior work (a named phenomenon, a specific failure condition, or a designed diagnostic such as targeted robustness checks) rather than a generic complaint. Score 5 if the gap is stated but only in vague terms ('existing methods have limitations'). Score 0 if no gap in prior work is characterized at all.
proposals.rationale: R55 identifies and names the specific 'overthinking' collapse phenomenon in iterated recurrent 'thinking systems,' and R13 designs 'ten diverse robustness checks designed to uncover fundamental weaknesses' rather than asserting weakness abstractly -- both dense_high_card_low. Precision of problem diagnosis is a real quality signal that generic 'motivates a gap' scorecard items likely flatten.

proposals.name: Absence of self-promotional hype language
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract's prose is sober and lets results speak for themselves, with no unearned superlatives, mission-statement rhetoric, or self-labeling of the work as a 'breakthrough'/'novel and powerful' etc. Score 5 if there is mild promotional language but it is largely backed by evidence. Score 0 if the abstract contains multiple instances of unsupported hype phrasing (e.g., calling its own idea a 'breakthrough,' declaring a research area 'conspicuously underexplored,' framing the work as a 'mission').
proposals.rationale: R46 literally states 'The breakthrough is based on...' about its own method, and R19 opens with 'we embark on a mission to craft...' and calls activation-function design 'conspicuously underexplored' -- both dense_low_card_high. This kind of self-congratulatory framing can inflate scorecard sub-scores tied to keywords like 'novelty' or 'significance' while a holistic reader discounts it as noise.

proposals.name: Internal naming consistency across method and artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if every name/acronym the abstract uses for its own method is used consistently, including in any linked code-repository name, with no unexplained mismatch. Score 5 if there is a minor inconsistency that doesn't affect understanding. Score 0 if the method's stated name clearly does not match the name of its own linked repository or other self-referenced artifact, suggesting careless drafting or leftover text from an earlier version.
proposals.rationale: R09 names its method 'Flat Hilbert Bayesian Inference (FHBI)' but links a repo titled '...Flat-Hilbert-Variational-Inference...', and R34 names its method 'CoPS (Cross-Task Experience Sharing)' but links a repo titled 'AlphaMemory' -- both dense_low_card_high. This is a concrete, checkable sloppiness signal a holistic reader would notice but which no plausible fixed rubric item would capture.

proposals.name: Stated mechanistic hypothesis for why the method works
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract offers an explicit causal/mechanistic hypothesis for why the proposed technique should improve results (not just that it does), stated as a reasoned claim about mechanism. Score 5 if a mechanism is gestured at but not clearly articulated. Score 0 if the abstract only reports that a method 'improves performance' with no account of why.
proposals.rationale: R31 states 'We hypothesize that randomly masking past tokens prevents over-attending to recent tokens and encourages attention to tokens in the distant past,' and R55 explains its design rationale ('keeps an explicit copy of the problem instance in memory so that it cannot be forgotten') -- both dense_high_card_low. A stated why-it-works account is a distinct quality signal from a stated that-it-works result.

proposals.name: Demonstrated cross-task or cross-architecture method generality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract provides concrete evidence (not just a claim) that the method transfers across multiple distinct tasks, architectures, or knowledge types, e.g. by naming several settings it was actually tested in. Score 5 if generality is asserted ('plug-and-play', 'broadly applicable') without supporting cross-setting evidence. Score 0 if the method is validated in exactly one narrow setting with no generality claim.
proposals.rationale: R07's K-Adapter is tested with two different kinds of injected knowledge across three knowledge-driven tasks/six datasets, and R25's MasKD is shown to work on both object detection and semantic segmentation 'without priors of ground-truth labels' -- both dense_high_card_low. This is generality backed by evidence, distinguishable from bare plug-and-play language (e.g. R02, dense_low_card_high, claims 'lightweight enough to plug and play' with no cross-setting evidence given), a distinction a scorecard keyed on the phrase itself would miss.

proposals.name: Named, quantified comparison against the strongest baseline
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a specific, currently-strong competing method or baseline by name and reports a precise quantified margin over it. Score 5 if it reports beating 'baselines' or 'state-of-the-art' generically with numbers but no named competitor. Score 0 if no comparison numbers are given at all.
proposals.rationale: R48 reports '31.03 BLEU... with over 2.6 BLEU improvement over the strong Transformer baseline' and sets records on three named benchmarks, and R49 reports '2x fewer learnable parameters' specifically 'compared to the prevailing fine-tuning technique LoRA' -- both dense_high_card_low. Naming the specific rival method being beaten, not just an unnamed 'baseline,' signals the authors situated their gain within the actual competitive landscape.

proposals.name: Concrete real-world stakes beyond benchmark numbers
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract articulates a specific downstream consequence or use case for why the capability matters beyond improving a leaderboard number (e.g., a named application domain or a step toward a broader human-relevant capability). Score 5 if 'real-world importance' is asserted only in boilerplate terms. Score 0 if no motivation beyond benchmark performance is given.
proposals.rationale: R04 frames its contribution as 'a step toward human-aligned understanding of visual abstractions' tied to how humans actually reason, and R37 motivates scientific image generation as 'a critical application for accelerating scientific progress' -- both dense_high_card_low. This kind of concrete, non-generic stakes-articulation is a judgment call a fixed rubric item is unlikely to reward specifically.

proposals.name: Single coherent problem-to-result throughline
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reads as one coherent narrative arc (a single problem motivates a single core insight that motivates the method and its evaluation). Score 5 if there are a couple of loosely related sub-contributions bolted together. Score 0 if the abstract reads as a disjointed list of several separate sub-components/contributions/tasks with no unifying thread.
proposals.rationale: R31 is a tight single-idea abstract (one masking idea, one mechanism hypothesis, one headline result), dense_high_card_low, versus R58, dense_low_card_high, which stitches together a new dataset, a named synthesis framework, and a separately-benchmarked VAD task with a distinct 'findings' paragraph -- three loosely joined pieces. Narrative coherence is plausibly something the dense reader rewards that a bank of independent, itemized criteria structurally cannot penalize (since each piece scores fine on its own).

proposals.name: Contextualized, not bare, quantitative improvement claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if large quantitative improvement claims (especially percentage figures) are accompanied by enough methodological context (what exactly is being measured, against what precise baseline condition) that the number is interpretable. Score 5 if numbers are given but the comparison basis is only loosely specified. Score 0 if headline percentage/speed numbers are presented with minimal context on what baseline or conditions produced them, giving a marketing-flyer feel.
proposals.rationale: R53 headlines '384% faster sampling times and 1822% reduced memory consumption' and R54 headlines '335.5 frames per second' with comparatively little methodological framing for those specific figures -- both dense_low_card_high. Contrast R17 (dense_high_card_low), which reports '1.24% root mean square error (RMSE)... 0.58% RMSE... r = 0.94' each tied to a precisely defined reconstruction procedure. A scorecard likely rewards the mere presence of large numbers rather than their interpretability.

proposals.name: Generalizable conceptual unification or named phenomenon
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract offers a general conceptual framework, a unifying principle across previously separate methods/tasks, or a newly named phenomenon that plausibly has explanatory reach beyond the specific benchmarks tested. Score 5 if the contribution is a solid but narrow point-fix to one method. Score 0 if the abstract presents only an incremental tweak with no broader conceptual claim.
proposals.rationale: R11 proposes representing statistical-model parameters as natural-language strings, unifying clustering, topic modeling, and regression under one interpretable framework with demonstrations across all three, and R55 both names the 'overthinking' phenomenon in iterated recurrent networks and proposes a general recall-architecture principle for 'thinking systems' broadly -- both dense_high_card_low. This kind of generative, transferable framing is a different axis of quality than any single scored criterion about one property of the method.

proposals.name: Mechanism-specific diagnosis of why prior methods fail
proposals.instruction: Score the causal specificity of the abstract's account of what is wrong with existing approaches, and whether the proposed fix is aimed at that exact mechanism. 10 = the abstract names a concrete mechanism ('layer norm normalizes within each token, so tokens at different positions become similar in magnitude, so positional context cannot be captured'; 'the refined Gaussian conditional and the hyperprior are mismatched, so rate cost inflates'), and the proposed method is visibly the counter to that mechanism. 5 = a limitation is named at the level of a symptom (slow, inaccurate, unstable) with no account of what produces it. 0 = the deficiency is stated only as an adoption or coverage fact ('X remains underexplored', 'ReLU persists', 'existing methods have limitations') with no mechanism at all. Judge only the text; do not reward length.
proposals.rationale: This is the sharpest visible split in the slice. R16 (dense .595 / card .090) and R06 (dense .683 / card .169) both spend their opening on a precise mechanical fault and then propose the exact counter-measure; R13 (dense .839 / card .316) does the same for 'overthinking' (the instance is forgotten across iterations, hence a recall architecture). On the other side R18 (dense .261 / card .790) diagnoses only that ReLU is still popular, and R28 (dense .156 / card .788) lists two symptoms (training uncertainty, head-class bias) without saying what causes them. A scorecard item like 'does the paper identify a limitation of prior work?' fires equally on all four; the mechanism grading separates them.

proposals.name: Headline number reported together with the baseline's number
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's central empirical claim is anchored: a specific quantity, on a named benchmark, with the comparison value it is being measured against. 10 = both endpoints are given, e.g. '55.7 to 59.2 on SuperGLUE', '40.9% WER versus 86.4%/92.9% for professional lipreaders and 89.8%/76.8% for prior systems', '35.44 BLEU on IWSLT 2014 De-En, +2.6 BLEU over a strong Transformer baseline'. 6 = own number given on a named benchmark but the baseline value is absent. 3 = a relative claim only ('substantial improvements', '3% higher'). 0 = 'consistently outperforms strong baselines', 'achieves state-of-the-art', 'notable margins', with no number anywhere. Do not reward more numbers; reward whether the reader can compute the delta.
proposals.rationale: R12 (dense .753 / card .133) and R22 (dense .692 / card .148) are both fully anchored, and R04 (dense .791 / card .013) is anchored three times over in a five-sentence abstract; the scorecard buries all three. Meanwhile R28 (card .788), R23 (dense .123 / card .819) and R18 (card .790) score high on the card while offering only 'outperforms previous works' / 'substantial improvements'. A generic 'reports experimental results' or 'compares to baselines' item cannot tell an anchored claim from an unanchored one; this criterion can.

proposals.name: Order-of-magnitude regime shift versus incremental delta
proposals.instruction: Score the size of the reported change relative to the operating range of the problem. 10 = the result moves the problem into a different regime that changes what is feasible: 1024-8192 sampling steps reduced to 4 at comparable perceptual quality; six benchmarks compressed to under 3% of their size while reconstructing the total score to 0.58% RMSE; a method scaled to graphs with hundreds of millions of nodes. 5 = a solid but within-regime improvement (a few points on a standard benchmark). 0 = an improvement of a size that would be indistinguishable from run-to-run variation or hyperparameter luck, or an improvement whose axis has no practical consequence. Score the magnitude claimed in the text, not the credibility of the claim (that is scored elsewhere).
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense .887 / card .360) and R42 (dense .787 / card .270) both report regime shifts, as does R55 (dense .814 / card .282); all three are under-credited by the scorecard. By contrast R39 (dense .005 / card .766) reports '3% higher than the winner' and R05 (dense .003 / card .889) reports statistically significant accuracy gains from re-tuning one hyperparameter — both read as fully-formed papers to a checklist but do not move the regime. Card-style items reward 'improvement demonstrated' as a binary; the dense model appears to be integrating how much.

proposals.name: Density of unanchored superlatives
proposals.instruction: Count the promotional phrases that carry no verifiable content ('extensive experiments', 'comprehensive evaluation', 'consistently outperforms', 'strong baselines', 'notable margins', 'significant improvements', 'remarkable', 'seamlessly', 'efficacy') and score INVERSELY as a fraction of the abstract's claim sentences. 10 = essentially none; every evaluative word is attached to a named object, number, or comparison. 5 = a few, mixed with anchored claims. 0 = the evaluative content of the abstract is carried almost entirely by such phrases, so that deleting them would leave no assessable claim. Long abstracts are not penalized per se; the score is the ratio, not the count.
proposals.rationale: R28 (dense .156 / card .788) and R24 (dense .031 / card .895) are near-saturated with this register ('comprehensive comparisons', 'consistently outperforms the baselines by notable margins', 'highlighting its practical efficacy'), as is R18 (card .790, 'adept and efficient', 'seamlessly', 'comprehensive experimentation underscores the efficacy'). The dense model puts all three in its bottom quartile. R14 (dense .894 / card .290) and R49 (dense .704 / card .112) are almost free of it. Judges scoring a bank of positively-worded criteria are, I suspect, partly reading this register as evidence for the property being scored — it is the cheapest thing in an abstract to fake.

proposals.name: One load-bearing idea versus stacked named sub-modules
proposals.instruction: Score whether the contributions cohere into one mechanism or are an assortment of separately-named additions. 10 = a single idea, stated once, that the whole paper is about; if there are two components, the abstract makes clear they are two halves of one mechanism serving one goal. 5 = two or three contributions with a stated but loose relation. 0 = a framework acronym containing two or more sub-acronyms, or a list of four or more heterogeneous contributions (a model, plus an augmentation trick, plus a visualization method, plus an extra analysis) with no argument that any of them requires the others. Penalize naming a component that is one heuristic; do not penalize naming the method itself.
proposals.rationale: R28 (dense .156 / card .788) is IKL = IUR + ICL, two unrelated heuristics under one umbrella name; R39 (dense .005 / card .766) stacks a classifier, a grad-CAM adaptation, an augmentation trick and an attention feedback loop; R53 (dense .136 / card .800) strings six separate claims. All three sit high on the card, because a bank scored per-property gets a hit on each item from a different contribution. R34 (dense .139 / card .722) and R14 (dense .894 / card .290) each carry exactly one idea. This is the clearest candidate for something the scorecard structurally over-credits: more named parts means more items fire.

proposals.name: Theory that constrains the method rather than decorating it
proposals.instruction: If the abstract claims theory, score whether the theory does work. 10 = the analysis produces the design (a derived mismatch motivates the specific regularizer; a derived relation between two algorithms yields the unified model; an estimator is derived and then its reconstruction error is measured), or it makes a prediction the experiments then check. 5 = correct-sounding theory adjacent to but not binding on the method. 0 = a theorem statement that restates the obvious ('performance depends on the quality of the pretrained model and on distribution matching'), or a generality claim ('we extend the analysis from finite-dimensional to infinite-dimensional spaces') with no consequence anywhere else in the abstract. Score 5 by default if no theory is claimed, so that empirical papers are not punished.
proposals.rationale: R06 (dense .683 / card .169) derives the mismatch and the fix follows from it; R42 (dense .787 / card .270) derives estimators and then reports their reconstruction RMSE; R36 (dense .909 / card .318) builds a bootstrap procedure for exactly the inferential setting it then uses. Against these, R15 (dense .073 / card .685) offers a theorem that is nearly a tautology and R24 (dense .019... card .895) advertises a Hilbert-space extension whose only consequence is a VTAB-1K table. A card item reading 'is the approach theoretically grounded?' cannot distinguish these; the presence of theory language is what it detects.

proposals.name: Reports its own negative results, failure modes, or residual difficulty
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract states something that did not work, a limit of the contribution, or an unresolved difficulty, in its own voice. 10 = a headline negative or an explicit residual ('none of the methods is successful on this benchmark, though careful fine-tuning yields improvements; the benchmark remains challenging'; 'all models face challenges, especially for complex prompts'; 'we present early training results'). 5 = a scoping statement that limits applicability without conceding a failure. 0 = every claim in the abstract is positive and every experiment reported works. A concession invented to look modest but contradicted by the rest of the abstract scores 3, not 10.
proposals.rationale: R40 (dense .888 / card .383) and R50 (dense .864 / card .187) both report that their subject matter defeats the methods tested, and both are strongly preferred by the dense model while the card ranks them low — a bank of positively-phrased criteria has no way to award points for an admitted failure and may actively subtract. R11 (dense .635 / card .080) volunteers 'early training results' and R32 (dense .732 / card .072) reports a surprise that is unflattering to the standard choice. Uniformly-positive abstracts such as R24 (card .895) and R30 (dense .249 / card .854) are exactly the ones the card over-credits.

proposals.name: Finding revises a belief many people act on
proposals.instruction: Score the abstract's central claim on how much it should change what a practitioner does. 10 = an established default is shown to be wrong or unnecessary in a way that touches many downstream choices (a vision-only encoder without text alignment beats the near-universal choice on fine-grained tasks; six widely-used benchmarks are shown to be largely redundant and reducible to a single common factor; the standard proxy for a target quantity is shown to have a large gap against the quantity itself across 611 models). 5 = a real reversal confined to one hyperparameter or one narrow setting. 0 = the finding is what anyone would have predicted from the setup (adding a regularizer improves the metric it regularizes; more data helps). Reward the substantiated reversal, not the word 'surprisingly'.
proposals.rationale: R32 (dense .732 / card .072), R42 (dense .787 / card .270) and R59 (dense .875 / card .323) all report reversals with broad reach and are all under-ranked by the card. The instructive boundary case is R05 (dense .003 / card .889), which explicitly announces 'contrary to previous findings' and is a genuine reversal — but only about the bootstrap rate of one classifier family, which is why I score reach rather than the presence of a contrast. A 'novelty' item on a card fires on both R05 and R32; this one should not.

proposals.name: Breadth of the claim matched by breadth of the demonstration
proposals.instruction: Compare the scope the abstract claims to the scope it evidences, and score the match. 10 = a plug-in or general-purpose claim is backed by demonstration across several distinct host systems or task families named in the text (dropped into ViT, Swin and PVT; three knowledge-driven tasks across six datasets plus probing; 3D grounding benchmarks plus general 2D grounding plus VQA suites). 5 = a claim of moderate scope evidenced on one family. 0 = a universal claim ('customizing to any downstream task seamlessly'; 'used in language models, RL, VAE, GAN, and neural architecture search') evidenced on a single task family or a microbenchmark. Score the ratio: a modest claim modestly evidenced scores 7, not 3.
proposals.rationale: R16 (dense .595 / card .090) and R27 (dense .864 / card .228) both earn their generality claims explicitly, and R37 (dense .856 / card .268) reports both its target domain and the general benchmarks where it stays competitive; the card discounts all three. R18 (dense .261 / card .790) promises 'any downstream task' and shows node- and link-level graph tasks, and R30 (dense .249 / card .854) invokes five application areas and evaluates sampling speed. A card item asking 'is the method general?' rewards the claim; this asks whether the claim was paid for.

proposals.name: Released artifact with its magnitude stated
proposals.instruction: Score the concreteness and size of the resource the paper contributes. 10 = a resource with its scale and composition named in the text (340M images annotated with pose, depth and surface normal; 3,886 hours of paired video and text; 206,339 human judgments across three modalities plus all modeling results; 25 fully pretrained checkpoints plus 140 intermediate ones and a statistical library). 5 = a resource named and available but with no stated scale. 2 = a bare promise of future release. 0 = no artifact. Judge only what the abstract states; do not credit an availability URL as scale.
proposals.rationale: R35 (dense .897 / card .079), R22 (dense .692 / card .148), R59 (dense .875 / card .323) and R36 (dense .909 / card .318) are the four largest artifact contributions in the slice and the card ranks all four low. Conversely R41 (dense .105 / card .633) and R28 (card .788) offer only a promise of code, and R19 (dense .038 / card .632) names five environments with no stated scale and no results, yet all sit high on the card. R10 (dense .361 / card .908) is the informative boundary: a real first-of-its-kind dataset whose size — participants, hours, recordings — is never stated.

proposals.name: Efficiency claim stated with its base and its quality condition
proposals.instruction: Score cost, speed and memory claims on whether they are interpretable and whether quality is held fixed. 10 = the cost is given in absolute, checkable terms together with the condition under which it holds ('3 minutes to judge 5K samples with 8 A100 GPUs'; 'the full distillation procedure does not take more time than training the original model'; '2-10x reduction in memory while matching or outperforming prior methods'). 5 = a ratio against a named baseline with no absolute anchor. 0 = an unanchored percentage or a raw throughput figure with no base, no hardware, and no statement of what happens to quality ('up to 384% faster and 1822% reduced memory'; '335.5 frames per second'). Score 5 by default if no efficiency claim is made.
proposals.rationale: R30 (dense .249 / card .854) and R38 (dense .010 / card .898) both lead on spectacular percentages with no interpretable base, and both are ranked near the top by the card and the bottom by the dense model; R25 (dense .194 / card .913), the single largest card score in the slice, is a 15-30x speedup with no absolute cost. R03 (dense .725 / card .066) and R01 (dense .887 / card .360) state cost in units a reader can verify. An 'is efficiency demonstrated?' item scores the loud version higher, which is backwards.

proposals.name: Core problem framed as a technical tension, not a coverage gap
proposals.instruction: Score how the paper motivates its problem. 10 = a genuine tension between two things that cannot both be maximized, stated concretely, with the method presented as a way to manage it (aligning to a personalized target while preserving text editability; more recurrent iterations should help but instead cause collapse; speech tokens capture linguistics but discard paralinguistics, and adding pitch alone does not close it; sample quality against number of sampling steps). 5 = a concrete difficulty stated without a competing objective. 0 = motivation is that a topic has not been studied ('conspicuously underexplored', 'remains an underexplored area', 'open-source environments have not advanced'). The tension must be technical; a tension between a field's ambitions and its funding does not count.
proposals.rationale: R17 (dense .700 / card .180), R13 (dense .839 / card .316) and R44 (dense .664 / card .114) all open on a real trade-off and all are under-ranked by the card, while R18 (dense .261 / card .790), R31 (dense .088 / card .869) and R19 (dense .038 / card .632) are motivated by absence-of-prior-work and sit high on it. Novelty items on a bank arguably reward the gap framing directly, since 'no one has done this' is the easiest form of novelty to assert and to verify.

proposals.name: Validation against the quantity actually cared about, including human data
proposals.instruction: Score whether the evaluation measures the thing the paper claims to care about rather than a convenient proxy. 10 = the target quantity is measured directly, with human judgment collected when the target is a human-facing property, and the collection described concretely (11 scientists rating on correctness, relevance and scientific accuracy; human ratings along established quality dimensions plus ten robustness checks; human-labeled question-answer pairs for the new benchmark; human similarity judgments as the criterion rather than a DNN stand-in). 5 = an automatic metric that is a well-accepted stand-in for the target. 0 = a benchmark number substituted for a target the abstract itself framed in human or deployment terms, with no acknowledgment of the substitution.
proposals.rationale: Four of the highest dense percentiles in the slice — R50 (dense .864 / card .187), R40 (dense .888 / card .383), R59 (dense .875 / card .323) and R45 (dense .894 / card .290) — all ground their headline in human measurement, and the card ranks every one of them below its dense rank. Human data is expensive and cannot be produced by a method-shaped paper, so it may be exactly the kind of evidence a criterion bank written around method properties has no slot for.

proposals.name: Grandest sentence matched by the evidence sentence
proposals.instruction: Locate the abstract's most ambitious claim and its strongest piece of evidence, and score the gap between them. 10 = the two are the same size; a modest claim with matching evidence scores 10 just as a large claim with large evidence does. 3 = the ambition sentence outruns the evidence by roughly one level (a framework claim supported by one task family). 0 = a sweeping claim about the field, the community, or a first-ever bridge between areas, supported by an experiment described in a single clause ('the first work that bridges pruning with the theory of differential privacy' evidenced by an inversion attack on two benchmark datasets; 'acts as a whistleblower for the community'; 'we hope to advance state-of-the-art research and inspire researchers', with no results reported at all). Penalize the gap, never the modesty.
proposals.rationale: R29 (dense .118 / card .754), R58 (dense .090 / card .918) and R19 (dense .038 / card .632) all pair field-level rhetoric with thin or absent evidence and are all ranked high by the card; R58 has the second-highest card percentile in the whole slice. R14 (dense .894 / card .290), R49 (dense .704 / card .112) and R56 (dense .735 / card .096) claim exactly what they show. Ambition and evidence are almost certainly scored by separate card items, so a paper can bank the ambition points without paying for them; scoring the ratio closes that.

proposals.name: Positioned against the nearest named prior method, not the field
proposals.instruction: Score the precision of the paper's positioning. 10 = the closest existing method is named, its specific behavior is characterized, and the contribution is stated as a difference from it ('in contrast to parallel WaveNet, we distill a Gaussian inverse autoregressive flow by minimizing a regularized KL divergence computed in closed form'; 'we extend the hybrid latent refinement method, which is designed for in-domain inference and degrades on rate cost cross-domain'; 'on each of the benchmark tasks proposed by Schwarzschild et al.'). 5 = a family of prior work named without a specific comparison point. 0 = positioning against an undifferentiated field ('existing methods', 'previous works', 'traditional approaches') with no named neighbor anywhere.
proposals.rationale: R14 (dense .894 / card .290) and R06 (dense .683 / card .169) both position against a single named neighbor and inherit its evaluation setting, as does R13 (dense .839 / card .316); the card ranks all three low. R23 (dense .123 / card .819) and R28 (card .788) position only against 'previous works'. Precise positioning is a signal of having actually read the neighborhood, and it is invisible to any item that asks whether related work is discussed — 'existing approaches often rely on X' satisfies that item at zero cost. R21 (dense .169 / card .780) is the boundary case: it names a comparison number (58.90 AUC-ROC for the second-best attack) but never names the method, so it should land mid-scale.

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanatory bridge
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives a coherent causal account linking the proposed mechanism to the claimed improvement; score 0 when it only lists components and reports results without explaining why they should work.
proposals.rationale: R01 connects distribution mismatch to rate cost and regularization; R02 connects distilled data to cost-surface minima. These mechanistic bridges may be under-credited by a criterion checklist.

proposals.name: Bottleneck-to-design fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method directly targets a sharply identified technical bottleneck with a correspondingly specific design; score 0 when the problem statement and proposed technique are weakly connected or generic.
proposals.rationale: R10 targets recurrent overthinking with explicit memory and iteration-invariant training; R51 targets source-data access constraints with a one-time density-processing scheme.

proposals.name: Cross-setting stress coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are tested across substantially different datasets, domains, tasks, or operating regimes; score 0 when evidence comes from one narrow setting with no stated variation.
proposals.rationale: R14 spans languages, tasks, and multiple optimization recipes; R33 evaluates 611 models across image, audio, and video domains. Such breadth distinguishes robust research from a single benchmark result.

proposals.name: Controlled contribution attribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract clearly isolates the effects of individual components, variants, or design choices through controlled comparisons; score 0 when the full system is presented without evidence identifying which parts matter.
proposals.rationale: R22 separates shallow features, DINO, and the final merging strategy; R36 contrasts pitch-based features with automatically learned paralinguistic attributes. This attributional clarity is evidence beyond headline performance.

proposals.name: Efficiency-quality frontier
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract quantifies resource savings together with preserved or improved task quality under a fair comparison; score 0 when efficiency is asserted vaguely or quality gains require unreported resource increases.
proposals.rationale: R03 pairs orders-of-magnitude faster inference with better detection; R20 reports memory reductions alongside explicit computation overhead. Dense judgments may notice the substantive tradeoff more than generic scorecard criteria do.

proposals.name: Shift and transfer robustness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly addresses unseen domains, objects, tasks, distributions, or conditions and demonstrates transfer across them; score 0 when it is evaluated only in the same conditions used for development.
proposals.rationale: R01 focuses on cross-domain compression; R25 estimates shapes of newly encountered objects from sparse observations; R48 analyzes distribution-matched experience transfer across tasks.

proposals.name: Minimal intervention, broad leverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a small, clearly specified change integrates with existing systems and improves several architectures or tasks with little added cost; score 0 when the method requires a large bespoke pipeline or its reuse is unspecified.
proposals.rationale: R05 replaces normalization layers across several vision transformers; R32 uses simple augmentations and removes negative examples while scaling to large graphs; R54 adds modular adapters without changing original parameters.

proposals.name: Diagnostic benchmark quality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a new dataset or benchmark is designed to expose meaningful failure modes, remove uninformative or leaking cases, and support interpretable evaluation; score 0 when it is mainly a larger collection of routine examples.
proposals.rationale: R15 combines human dimensions with robustness checks and contextual presentation; R17 tests spatial, numeric, and attribute composition; R29 filters uninformative samples and answer leakage.

proposals.name: Claim specificity and calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims specify datasets, metrics, baselines, magnitudes, and operating conditions, while limiting conclusions to what the evidence supports; score 0 when claims are vague, absolute, or unsupported by concrete scope.
proposals.rationale: R18 gives window conditions, multiple metrics, and quantified gains; R46 states mathematical equivalence and precise speed and memory changes. In contrast, broad superiority language without scope is easier for a scorecard to over-credit.

proposals.name: Boundary and failure disclosure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract explicitly identifies limitations, difficult cases, tradeoffs, or conditions where methods fail; score 0 when it presents only unqualified success claims.
proposals.rationale: R15 reports that existing metrics fail its challenging benchmark; R17 states that all evaluated models struggle with compositional prompts; R38 reports that the optimal sampling regime depends on the dataset.

proposals.name: Theory-to-method closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when theoretical analysis yields a concrete algorithmic choice or design principle that is then empirically examined; score 0 when theory and experiments are disconnected or theory is merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R09 turns alignment theory into a cross-covariance graph operator; R39 derives a view of SGD that motivates Weighted SGD; R59 links pruning to differential-privacy noise and tests the connection.

proposals.name: Compositional capability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method combines multiple capabilities or representations so that their interaction enables a qualitatively broader target behavior; score 0 when components operate independently without an integrated capability claim.
proposals.rationale: R42 composes schemas, hierarchical grounding, and visual reasoning for abstract concepts; R50 combines 2D and 3D perception with multimodal prompting and varied interfaces; R52 integrates tool selection, visual input, and tool-result aggregation.

proposals.name: Procedure-level generality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract distinguishes conclusions about a training procedure from a single trained artifact and evaluates variation across seeds, checkpoints, models, or implementations; score 0 when conclusions rest on one unreplicated instance.
proposals.rationale: R24 explicitly studies 25 checkpoints and bootstrap inference across training variation; R33 evaluates hundreds of pretrained models; R14 compares multiple complete training recipes rather than one configuration.

proposals.name: Conceptual reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work reveals a useful new interpretation, connection, or hidden assumption that changes how an established problem can be understood; score 0 when it is only an incremental component substitution with no conceptual insight.
proposals.rationale: R02 reframes one-step distillation as movement toward true-task minima; R13 unifies label propagation and graph convolution through smoothing and influence; R59 reframes pruning as potentially privacy-enhancing.

proposals.name: Real-world constraint alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract grounds the problem, method, and evaluation in concrete operational constraints or realistic data collection and deployment conditions; score 0 when practical relevance is asserted without such constraints or evidence.
proposals.rationale: R11 addresses scaling unstructured weather observations; R16 uses rover navigation and Curiosity data; R44 contributes a publicly accessible bilingual brain-signal dataset with application-oriented benchmarks.

proposals.name: Failure-to-mechanism fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mode and the proposed mechanism directly addresses it with matching evidence; score 0 when the problem and method are only loosely connected or no failure mode is specified.
proposals.rationale: R09 diagnoses a distribution mismatch and designs distribution regularization for it; R38 links Layer Normalization's limitation to a specific inter-token normalization remedy; R51 targets overthinking with explicit memory and iteration-invariant training.

proposals.name: Explanatory mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method's behavior is explained by an interpretable, testable mechanism linking representations or objectives to outcomes; score 0 when the abstract presents only an architectural recipe.
proposals.rationale: R06 explains how natural-language predicates become statistical features; R22 connects structural representations to coherent human-image generation; R46 explains abstraction through hierarchical schema grounding.

proposals.name: Non-obvious discovery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the paper reports a surprising, non-trivial finding that changes the design or interpretation and validates it; score 0 when the contribution is merely an expected incremental improvement.
proposals.rationale: R08 discovers that benchmark items can be sparsely compressed while preserving scores; R10 finds that non-text-aligned DINO features can outperform CLIP for fine-grained perception; R19 finds that existing referenceless metrics fail its context-sensitive evaluation.

proposals.name: Breadth of validation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method is evaluated across multiple independent tasks, datasets, domains, or operating conditions with consistent evidence; score 0 when it is tested in one narrow setting.
proposals.rationale: R05 evaluates knowledge adapters across six datasets and three task types; R16 varies across 25 checkpoints and studies a downstream bias question; R56 evaluates 611 models across image, audio, and video domains.

proposals.name: Stress-test coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation deliberately probes distribution shifts, perturbations, difficult subcases, or known failure modes tied to the claim; score 0 when only a standard aggregate benchmark is reported.
proposals.rationale: R19 includes ten robustness checks and context-dependent human quality dimensions; R48 varies spatial, numeric, and attribute composition across languages and output modes, exposing failures on complex prompts.

proposals.name: Stability under variation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract directly measures variation across seeds, checkpoints, models, raters, or samples and reports stability or uncertainty; score 0 when conclusions rest on one unexamined run or checkpoint.
proposals.rationale: R16 is motivated by checkpoint variability and introduces MultiBERTs plus Multi-Bootstrap inference; R56 compares hundreds of pretrained models and extensive human judgments rather than relying on a single artifact.

proposals.name: Quantified efficiency-quality tradeoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a resource reduction is quantified alongside preserved or improved task quality at meaningful scale; score 0 when efficiency or quality is claimed without measuring the other side.
proposals.rationale: R24 reduces diffusion sampling to four steps while retaining strong FID and reports training cost; R30 reports orders-of-magnitude faster anomaly inference while outperforming DDPM; R41 combines 2–10x lower memory with large-graph performance.

proposals.name: Portable intervention
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the same intervention transfers across architectures, tasks, or domains with low overhead and little bespoke redesign; score 0 when it works only in one setup or requires extensive specialization.
proposals.rationale: R09 integrates its refinement into existing test-time compression methods across in-domain and cross-domain data; R38 replaces normalization layers across ViT, Swin, and PVT; R44 applies masked distillation to both detection and segmentation.

proposals.name: Component attribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when ablations isolate each component's contribution and demonstrate meaningful complementarity; score 0 when only the complete system is compared against baselines.
proposals.rationale: R05 reports separate and combined adapter gains; R06 finds both continuous relaxation and iterative refinement crucial; R10 evaluates the distinct roles of shallow features, DINO, CLIP, and their merger.

proposals.name: Constraint-aware design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method is explicitly designed for a concrete practical constraint and that constraint is evaluated; score 0 when applicability is merely asserted without constrained evidence.
proposals.rationale: R18 builds persistent image-conditioned tool use for real-world multimodal tasks; R34 addresses personalization from few target images while preserving editability; R58 adapts without access to source data because of privacy constraints.

proposals.name: Construct-aligned evaluation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation measures the stated construct with human judgments or task-specific correctness checks and identifies proxy-metric failures; score 0 when it relies only on generic automatic scores.
proposals.rationale: R19 uses human ratings across quality dimensions and tests whether referenceless metrics reflect them; R48 uses scientists to assess correctness, relevance, and scientific accuracy rather than image similarity alone.

proposals.name: Reusable research asset
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract offers a clearly reusable dataset, model suite, benchmark, or tool together with scope that enables follow-up research; score 0 when release is vague, merely promised, or absent.
proposals.rationale: R16 releases multiple checkpoints and statistical software; R48 provides a benchmark spanning scientific concepts, languages, and generation modes; R56 releases similarity and language data with 206,339 judgments and modeling results.

proposals.name: Theory-to-design loop
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when analysis yields a concrete design choice or falsifiable prediction that experiments test, including informative failures; score 0 when theory consists of disconnected bounds or guarantees without tested consequences.
proposals.rationale: R09 uses its marginalization analysis to motivate distribution regularization and evaluates it; R20 combines theoretical guarantees for a neural influence kernel with synthetic and real-data tests; this contrasts with abstract-only bounds such as R52.

proposals.name: Contribution coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one coherent contribution explains why each component is needed and how the parts fit together; score 0 when many branded modules are stacked with weakly articulated roles.
proposals.rationale: R01 combines a hybrid network, augmentation, visualization, window studies, and attention without a single clearly unified causal story; R21 similarly layers progressive generation and autoregression; R27 introduces multiple named components with limited mechanistic linkage.

proposals.name: Evidence specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are anchored by named baselines, datasets, metrics, effect sizes, and evaluation conditions; score 0 when the abstract relies mainly on generic claims of state-of-the-art or significant superiority.
proposals.rationale: R04 claims superiority on real graphs without concrete comparisons or magnitudes; R26 reports substantial improvements across tasks but gives little quantitative evidence; R60 reports only notable margins despite naming many baselines.
